draft.title: The Anzac legend
card: The Anzac legend is a story Australians tell about their soldiers at Gallipoli and on other fronts. It praises mateship, courage and endurance.
Mateship means looking after your mates. Endurance means putting up with hardship. The legend presents these as typical Australian qualities.
Historians point out that the legend can leave people out. Women who served as nurses and First Nations soldiers are often missing from the story.
Historians also debate how much the legend shaped national identity, which is how Australians see themselves as a nation. Some say it shaped it a great deal. Others say it is only one part.
draft.remember: The Anzac legend praises soldiers' qualities, but historians question who it leaves out and how much it shaped identity.

a.q: Which question would a historian ask when studying the Anzac legend?
opts: Whose experiences does the story leave out?
Which battle did Australia lose most heavily?
Why did the soldiers dislike their officers?
How many soldiers enlisted from each state?
a.why: The card says historians debate whom the legend leaves out, such as women and First Nations soldiers. The other questions are about war history, but they are not the debate about the legend itself.
a.clue: Think about what the legend includes and what it may miss.

b.q: A school assembly says the Anzac story shows all Australians in 1915 were brave and united. Why might a historian question this?
opts: It can leave out people such as nurses and First Nations soldiers
It suggests that soldiers showed courage and endurance
It describes mateship as a quality of Australian soldiers
It says the story is told by Australians about themselves
b.why: The legend can leave out people whose service did not fit the picture, so it may not show all Australians. Praising courage, endurance or mateship is what the legend does, so that alone is not the historian's concern.
b.clue: Look for the option about who is missing from the story.
